title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, ask about someone else's, and use possessives (my, your, Rina's) and plurals.
intro:
Bengali kinship words are wonderfully precise: there are different words for your mother's brother (মামা) and your father's brother (কাকা / চাচা), and the words often differ between Hindu/West Bengal and Muslim/Bangladeshi families. Family words are also used for strangers as polite terms of address.

Grammatically you'll learn the **possessive ending -র / -এর** and the **plural endings -রা and -গুলো**. There is **no gender** to worry about.

vocab.note: Also আম্মা / আম্মু (amma / ammu) in Bangladesh.
Also আব্বা / আব্বু (abba / abbu) in Bangladesh.
In Bangladesh also the word for 'elder brother' and a polite address for any man.
Watch out: the same word means different relatives in Kolkata and Dhaka!
Polite address for a slightly older woman.
Same in WB and BD. Also used for rickshaw-pullers and shopkeepers in Dhaka!
Also কাকু (kaku), common for any older man.
Unmarried: অবিবাহিত. Colloquial: বিয়ে হয়েছে 'has got married'.

phrases.native: আমার এক ভাই আর দুই বোন আছে।
phrases.roman: amar æk bhai ar dui bon achhe.
phrases.en: I have one brother and two sisters.
Do you have brothers and sisters?
How many children do you have?

grammar.title: Possessives: -র / -এর and possessive pronouns
grammar.body:
To say *X's*, add **-র** (*-r*) after a vowel and **-এর** (*-er*) after a consonant: মা → **মার** / মায়ের 'mother's', রিনা → **রিনার** 'Rina's', বাবা → **বাবার**, ভাই → **ভাইয়ের** (*bhaiyer*), দেশ → **দেশের**. The possessor comes **first**: বাবার নাম 'father's name'.

Possessive pronouns:
আমার *amar* my – আমাদের *amader* our
তোর *tor* your (intimate) – তোদের *toder*
তোমার *tomar* your (familiar) – তোমাদের *tomader*
আপনার *apnar* your (respectful) – আপনাদের *apnader*
তার / ওর *tar / or* his, her – তাদের / ওদের
তাঁর / ওনার *taṃr / onar* his, her (respectful)

**'To have'**: Bengali has no verb 'have'. Say **X-র ... আছে** 'of X ... exists': আমার একটা গাড়ি আছে 'I have a car'. The negative is **নেই**: আমার গাড়ি নেই.

grammar.title: Plurals: -রা, -গুলো, -দের
grammar.body:
Bengali nouns have **no gender**, and often no plural marking when the meaning is clear or a number is used (দুই বোন 'two sisters').

For **people**, add **-রা** (*-ra*) after a vowel, **-েরা** (*-era*) after a consonant: ছেলে → ছেলেরা 'the boys', বন্ধু → বন্ধুরা, লোক → লোকেরা. The plural possessive is **-দের** (*-der*) / **-েদের**: ছেলেদের 'the boys''.

For **things and animals** (and colloquially people too), use the classifier **-গুলো** (*-gulo*) 'the …s': বইগুলো 'the books'. Possessive: বইগুলোর.

A few nouns have a gendered form, mainly borrowed from Sanskrit (ছাত্র / ছাত্রী student), but adjectives and verbs never change.

dialogue.title: Looking at family photos
dialogue.setting: Anika shows her friend Jake photos of her family in Dhaka on her phone.

lines.speaker: Anika
lines.native: উনি আমার নানি। আর এ আমার নানা।
lines.roman: uni amar nani. ar e amar nana.
lines.en: She's my (maternal) grandmother. And this is my grandfather.

lines.speaker: Anika
lines.native: মা, বাবা, আমার এক ভাই আর এক বোন।
lines.roman: ma, baba, amar æk bhai ar æk bon.
lines.en: Mum, Dad, one brother and one sister.

lines.speaker: Anika
lines.en: His name is Rafi. He's a student.

lines.speaker: Anika
lines.native: উনি আমার খালু, মানে খালার স্বামী।
lines.roman: uni amar khalu, mane khalar shami.
lines.en: He's my uncle, I mean my aunt's husband.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.en: You have a lot of relatives!

culture: Using people's first names is reserved for equals and juniors. Older siblings are called দাদা/দিদি (WB) or ভাইয়া/আপু (BD), never by name. Strangers become relatives too: a shopkeeper is দাদা or ভাই, an older woman মাসিমা or খালা, and in Dhaka a rickshaw-puller is often called মামা. Hindu and Muslim families use different words for many relatives (কাকা/চাচা, মাসি/খালা, পিসি/ফুফু, ঠাকুমা/দাদি), and in Bangladesh দাদা means 'grandfather', not 'brother'.
